In brief

Telemachus opens with a flurry of Grecian echoes: "InTROIbo," "Chrysostomos," one Irishman's "ancient Greek" name, another's "Hellenic"-sounding double dactyls. This soundscape serves Joyce's purpose of making readers think about the literary antecedents of Ulysses, but it also characterizes the relationship between the two main characters in the chapter. Mulligan has barely begun talking to Stephen before he proposes that they take a trip to Greece together: "We must go to Athens. Will you come if I can get the aunt to fork out twenty quid?" A little later he says, "Ah, Dedalus, the Greeks! I must teach you. You must read them in the original." Many interesting subtexts lurk within these sentences: Joyce's ambition to write a work as great as the Odyssey; his ignorance of Greek; his friend Gogarty's classical education at Trinity College; Oscar Wilde's trip to Greece; homosexuality ancient and modern; older men directing the cultural education of younger ones.

At more length

Joyce was a gifted linguist. The Jesuits taught him Latin, at which he excelled. He learned enough Dano-Norwegian to read Ibsen’s plays, enough French to live in Paris, enough Italian to live in Trieste, enough German to live in Zurich. Finnegans Wake contains echoes of roughly 70 languages. But the writer who modeled his great masterpiece on the Odyssey never learned classical Greek. In a June 1921 letter to Harriet Shaw Weaver he ruefully noted the fact:

I don’t even know Greek though I am spoken of as erudite. My father wanted me to take Greek as third language, my mother German and my friends Irish. Result, I took Italian. I spoke or used to speak modern Greek not too badly (I speak four or five languages fluently enough) and have spent a great deal of time with Greeks of all kinds from noblemen down to onionsellers, chiefly the latter. I am superstitious about them. They bring me luck.

Ellmann observes that he felt the same way about the Greek national colors in which the 1922 Ulysses was bound: the white letters on a sea-blue background brought him luck (524). But he could not read Homer "in the original," and he chose to inject this deficiency into his fiction by having Mullilgan offer to act as a kind of docent to Stephen: "I must teach you." Joyce makes Mulligan's ostentatious display of classical learning sound sophomorically pretentious—Epi oinopa ponton may be the most familiar ancient Greek phrase on the planet, and Thalatta! Thalatta! likewise is something that a beginning student of Greek might take away from his Xenophon—but he clearly knows more Greek than Stephen does.

This disparity reflects the much greater one that existed between Joyce and Oliver Gogarty, who had received an excellent classical education at Trinity College Dublin. Trinity's dons were renowned for learning and rigor, and since 1761 the college had boasted the Regius Professorship of Greek, a chair held in the late 19th century by John Kells Ingram and Robert Yelverton Tyrrell. Gogarty studied under Ingram, Tyrrell, John Pentland Mahaffy, and other dynamic scholars. His biographer Ulick O'Connor discusses his "extraordinary memory for Greek and Latin verse" and notes that it "fascinated Joyce" (68). Apparently he knew Greek well enough to carry on conversations in it: "Stephen McKenna, the translator of Plotinus, held open house, provided those who came conversed either in Irish or Greek" (141). Gogarty's remarkable facility at spinning out English verses owed much to his mastery of classical metrics and to the quickwitted example of men like Tyrrell and Mahaffy.

Joyce did not have access to an equally good classical education at University College Dublin. Gogarty had briefly attended that school just before Joyce arrived, but then he left for Trinity and quickly charmed its brilliant dons. That history, plus the fact that Joyce was four years younger than Gogarty, may account for the paternalistic way in which Mulligan chivvies Stephen toward all things Greek. It certainly explains his declaration that "We must go to Athens." Slote, Mamigonian, and Turner note that traveling to Greece "was apparently a fixation of Gogarty's during the time he was living at the Sandycove Martello Tower," and that fixation had a genesis in another brilliant classics student at Trinity, of the previous generation. Oscar Wilde, who is constantly on Mulligan's lips in Telemachus, had traveled to Athens in 1877.

After a secondary education that included intensive study of Latin and Greek, Wilde entered Trinity College in 1871 and excelled as a classicist under Tyrrell and Mahaffy. He left Trinity for Oxford after receiving a five-year scholarship in 1874, but in 1875 he accompanied Mahaffy on a trip to Italy, and in April 1877 the two men traveled to Greece. Mahaffy was keen to visit Athens and even more Mycenae, where in 1876 Heinrich Schliemann had excavated many gold artifacts, including the magnificent (supposed) mask of Agamemnon. It is surely no accident that Mulligan's wish to act as Stephen's teacher and go with him to Greece reproduces Mahaffy's plan of traveling with his most promising student. Many factors, starting with Wilde's notorious sexual orientation, conspire to create the impression that Mulligan may be considering Stephen as a potential sexual partner.

Mahaffy held the chair in Ancient History at Trinity, and in 1874 he published Social Life in Greece from Homer to Menander.  The book went through at least seven editions, but one of the observations in the first version—that ancient Greek men married women for purposes of procreation but took beautiful young men as lovers—proved so controversial that Mahaffy had to delete it from subsequent editions. Oscar Wilde helped edit the proofs of that first edition at Mahaffy's house in Howth and this young gay man must have felt excited and validated by the book's findings. There is no evidence that he had a sexual relationship his professor: Mahaffy, an ordained Anglican clergyman, married in 1865 and produced four children, and after Wilde's trial he disowned his former pupil. But even if the two men were not lovers, their association may well have struck some onlookers as an example of the kind of relationships that Mahaffy was writing about.

When Mulligan urges Stephen to learn Greek, he does not say that he would like to teach him the language, but rather, "Ah Dedalus, the Greeks! I must teach you." His emphasis on social life may reflect a knowledge of Mahaffy's book, but it might as easily derive from other sources that Gogarty encountered at Oxford University. Slote and his collaborators note that "At Oxford University in the late nineteenth century, various university reformers, such as the Classical scholar Benjamin Jowett (1817-93), sought to establish Hellenism as an alternative value system to Christian theology. Various of his students and followers of his movement used Greek writings to justify male love to such an extent that Hellenic studies, particularly at Oxford, became largely synonymous with homosexuality." When Mulligan says a bit later, "God, Kinch, if you and I could only work together we might do something for the island. Hellenise it," he may be speaking not only of a more general shift in cultural values from Hebraic moralism to Hellenic aestheticism but, more covertly, of the value of male-male love.

In Scylla and Charybdis the covert becomes overt, though Mulligan displaces it from himself onto others. Introducing "the charge of pederasty brought against the bard," he coos and flutters about Dowden's comment: "All we can say is that life ran very high in those days. Lovely!" Stephen responds with a silent, contemptuous thought about man-boy love: "Catamite." Near the end of the chapter Mulligan tells Stephen that he found Bloom bending over to examine a statue's rear cleavage: "O, I fear me, he is Greeker than the Greeks. His pale Galilean eyes were upon her mesial groove." Then he transfers the thought of anal intercourse to Stephen: "Did you see his eye? He looked upon you to lust after you. I fear thee, ancient mariner. O, Kinch, thou art in peril. Get thee a breechpad." Again Stephen responds with silent ridicule: "Manner of Oxenford." Clearly the culture of English schoolboy homosexuality that Jowett's followers had elevated into high cultural accomplishment is implicit in Mulligan's idea of becoming "Greek."

Stephen is not "thrilled" by Mulligan's touch in Telemachus as he was by Cranly's arm in A Portrait, but nor does he display homophobic revulsion or anger. In Proteus he does not judge the homosexual passion that landed Wilde in prison: "Staunch friend, a brother soul: Wilde's love that dare not speak its name. His arm: Cranly's arm. He now will leave me. And the blame? As I am. As I am. All or not at all." He seems afraid not of sex but of subordination. Anger flashed from him in Telemachus because of Mulligan's overbearing manner and casual unconcern: "O, it's only Dedalus whose mother is beastly dead." Whoever may be to "blame" for the resulting breach, Stephen will not tolerate an intimacy that does not accept him "As I am." Ancient Greek man-boy love involved a kind of trade: the older man's wisdom and sophistication for the younger man's sexual attractiveness. Mulligan seems to be stepping into this role—taking Stephen under his wing, aggressively advising him, presuming to know what is best for him. That is not the kind of paternity Stephen seeks, and the "manner of Oxenford" and Trinity—older men sniffily cultivating an elite crop of young bloomers—is not his idea of cultural vitality.

Wilde's famous wit was honed by hanging out with brilliant talkers like Tyrrell and Mahaffy, and the same was true of Gogarty. Mulligan's sparkling repartee in Telemachus is of a piece with what is known of these men's talk. When a women's rights activists asked Mahaffy what was the difference between a man and a woman he replied, "I can't conceive." When told that the current Provost, whom he hoped to succeed, had fallen ill, he remarked, "Nothing trivial, I hope?" James Joyce, he said, "is a living argument in defence of my contention that it was a mistake to establish a separate university for the aborigines of this island." Tyrrell too had a sharp tongue. Ulick O'Connor records his telling a bore at the dinner table, "Have some tongue, like cures like," and when someone interrupted one of his conversational flights by asking the way to the bathroom he said without turning, "The first door on the right marked 'gentlemen'—but don't let that deter you" (33).

This atmosphere of haughtily privileged, intellectually superior badinage can be heard in Mulligan's many cutting remarks. Stephen appears to tolerate it well enough when Mulligan is simply insulting other people, but he does not like being regarded as a reclamation project himself. The novel shows him in revolt against being treated as a sidekick—younger, less accomplished, and less enlightened, but full of promise if he can correct his flaws. If becoming "Greek" means falling under the sway of a benevolently paternal instructor, then Stephen wants no part of it.

But Joyce was surely of one mind with Gogarty in another way. His decision to model his epic on Homer proceeded from a determination to bring Ireland into the long European tradition of learning and art that began with the Greeks. Ellmann astutely observes that “Gogarty spoke of Hellenizing Ireland, Joyce (who knew no Greek) of Europeanizing it” (118). Ireland was a cultural backwater made stagnant by religious piety and colonial domination, and could not come into its own simply by turning inward. In the lecture titled "Ireland, Island of Saints and Sages" Joyce lamented the present intellectual stagnation of his country and expressed hope that it would "resume its ancient position as the Hellas of the north some day."

This note originally addressed only the question of Joyce's ignorance of ancient Greek. In a personal communication Vincent Van Wyk suggested that I expand it to include consideration of Oscar Wilde's 1877 trip, noting that Mulligan may be presuming to take on Mahaffy's role of teacher, thereby asserting "some sort of intellectual predominance" over Stephen—not to mention promoting a "Greek" understanding of sexuality. I agree entirely with Van Wyk's estimation of the trip's significance.

John Hunt 2026
